title: Digital learning and student outcomes: a mathematical synthesis from the last decade
venue: International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE)
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether digital learning improves students’ cognitive learning outcomes, and whether effects differ by intervention characteristics. The authors note conflicting prior findings and the need for a stronger quantitative synthesis of evidence before more recent AI-driven tools, such as ChatGPT, are widely integrated into education. To address this, they conducted a meta-analysis of randomized, pretest-posttest controlled studies published between 2013 and 2023.

The review included 17 studies with 1,896 participants across educational levels and subject areas. Interventions ranged from online quizzes and web-based e-learning to virtual reality, augmented reality, mobile learning apps, and learning platforms. Included studies covered primary, middle school, secondary, undergraduate, and graduate settings; outcomes were objective cognitive measures such as grades, knowledge tests, and skill assessments. The authors synthesized effects using a random-effects model and tested moderators including cognitive engagement mode, sample size, duration, setting, subject area, and tool usage environment.

Overall, digital learning showed a positive, moderate effect on cognitive outcomes compared with traditional instruction, and the publication-bias-adjusted estimate remained positive. Subgroup analyses suggested larger gains for active versus passive engagement and somewhat stronger effects in school settings, smaller samples, and shorter interventions, but none of these differences reached statistical significance. The authors conclude that digital learning can improve academic outcomes, yet the evidence base is highly heterogeneous and still too limited to support firm claims about which conditions produce the strongest effects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis of randomized controlled pretest-posttest studies with explicit inclusion criteria and quantitative synthesis. Although heterogeneity was high (I2=83%), the design and evidence synthesis quality are strong.
impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on cognitive outcomes was moderate and clearly positive (g=.62; adjusted g=.49), exceeding the threshold for medium impact. The review spans multiple subjects and levels, indicating meaningful general educational relevance rather than a niche effect.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analyzed digital learning and e-learning interventions delivered via software, online platforms, VR/AR apps, mobile apps, web-based courses, and other technology-supported instruction compared with traditional non-digital instruction; the paper treats these as technology-assisted learning conditions rather than a single specific product.

finding.finding_summary: Across 17 randomized pretest-posttest studies (n=1,896), digital learning interventions produced a positive moderate gain in cognitive learning outcomes versus traditional instruction. The pooled effect was Hedge’s g=.62 (95% CI .38 to .86, p<.01), and the trim-and-fill adjusted estimate remained positive at g=.49 (95% CI .40 to .59).
finding.measure: Objective cognitive learning outcomes / posttest academic achievement measures across subjects
